analysis.one_liner: Requires safety testing and public disclosure before chemical dispersants can be used on oil spills.
analysis.headline: Introduced months after the BP Deepwater Horizon spill, the bill drew no cosponsors, never got a hearing or vote, and died in committee when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Water Act so that no chemical dispersant could be used to break up an oil spill unless the EPA first determined, using health and environmental data, that spraying it causes less harm than letting the oil degrade or be cleaned up by other means. It would require dispersant makers to submit data on toxicity, effectiveness, and ingredients, require the EPA to make that information public, and order a federal study of whether the government has the ability to judge dispersant safety. It was introduced in September 2010, after the BP spill drew public attention to the little-tested dispersant Corexit, and never advanced past a subcommittee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the main beneficiaries would be people who live on or make a living from affected coastlines — fishing and seafood workers, tourism businesses, and residents — as well as cleanup workers and volunteers who handle dispersants directly, and emergency medical personnel and researchers who would gain access to ingredient and safety data currently treated as confidential. The bill would not ban dispersants; it would let them keep being used, but only after the EPA found them safer than the alternatives.

how_it_helps.text: No dispersant could be used on an oil spill unless the EPA listed it on the National Contingency Plan Product Schedule after finding it meets toxicity and effectiveness standards and causes less harm than letting the oil disperse, degrade, or be physically removed [S2][S3].

The EPA would have to weigh acute and chronic health effects, effects on workers and nearby residents, and how dispersants interact with oil, including persistence and bioaccumulation, before approving a product [S2][S3].

The bill requires the EPA to make all health and safety information on approved dispersants public, and ingredient concentrations where needed to protect public health, giving responders, local residents, medical personnel, and researchers access to data now held as confidential [S2][S3].

It orders a federal study, with public comment, of whether the government has adequate data and legal authority to judge dispersant health and environmental impacts, followed by a report to Congress and a decision on rewriting the dispersant rules in the National Contingency Plan [S2][S3].
The minimum data set would specifically cover effects on cleanup workers, volunteers, and people living near application areas, not just marine life [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The cost falls mainly on dispersant manufacturers, who would have to run extensive toxicity, effectiveness, and ingredient-combination tests and disclose safety information they now keep confidential. Oil and gas companies would bear the consequences of tighter limits on a cheap, standard spill-response tool, including the possibility that a favored dispersant could not be used in some conditions.

drawbacks.text: The bill's core test — that a dispersant must cause less harm than natural dispersion, degradation, or physical cleanup — could be difficult to establish quickly during an actual spill, and supporters of dispersant use argue that requiring a fully populated data set before listing a product could slow emergency response when speed matters [S3].

Dispersant manufacturers would bear significant testing and disclosure costs, and companies have objected on trade-secret grounds to publicizing ingredient concentrations, a conflict the bill resolves mostly in favor of disclosure [S2][S3].

The bill imposes new regulatory duties on the EPA with fixed deadlines (a 180-day study, a report, a decision on rewriting the rules within 270 days), which would require new agency capacity and could crowd out other priorities [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would not ban dispersants; it would require proof before their use and transparency about what is in them. The cost is real but narrow — testing expenses for a small number of manufacturers and some trade-secret loss — while the benefit is better information for the workers, residents, and responders most exposed during a major spill. A fair criticism is that rigid pre-approval requirements could complicate fast-moving emergency decisions, but the bill leaves the EPA discretion to set standards, which softens that risk.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and then to a subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote until the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the Safe Dispersants Act on September 14, 2010, about five months after the BP Deepwater Horizon disaster began, and it was referred the same day to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the House Energy and Commerce Committee [S1][S3][S5].
On September 15, 2010, it was referred to the Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee; that was the bill's last action of record [S5].
The bill attracted no cosponsors during its time in the House [S4].
It received no hearing, committee vote, or floor vote before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011, killing the bill [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Dispersant manufacturers are better off, since no new testing, toxicity standards, or ingredient disclosure requirements were imposed on them, and oil companies keep access to dispersants as a low-cost spill-response tool.

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Safe Dispersants Act and served as its sole sponsor.

against.name: James Oberstar
against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee leadership took no action on the bill after referral; it was sent to a subcommittee and never received a markup or vote.

against.name: Henry Waxman
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Committee leadership took no action on the bill after its secondary referral; no hearing or markup is recorded.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the record shows only a single Democratic sponsor and no recorded partisan positions either way.

industries.note: The bill would require makers of products like Corexit to prove toxicity and effectiveness against detailed standards, build a federal data set on ingredients and behavior in combination with oil, and disclose health and safety information publicly. That testing and disclosure burden is exactly what the companies avoided by the bill dying in committee.

The bill does not ban dispersants, but tighter listing standards could restrict when and where oil companies can use them, raising spill-response costs. Dispersants are attractive to spillers because they make oil disappear from the surface at low cost; more protective rules would shift some of that cost back to the industry.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing, seafood, and coastal tourism
industries.note: Better-tested, better-disclosed dispersants and a higher bar for their use would reduce the risk that a spill response itself damages fisheries and coastlines, as coastal communities charged happened during the BP spill. The bill's outcome leaves their exposure unchanged.
